newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Fund selling cuts 10 pct off coffee prices.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Fund selling cuts 10 pct off coffee prices.

text.p: Coffee markets were jolted on Tuesday as a big sell-off by speculative funds pared London futures prices for robusta beans by around 10 percent over the day.
London's benchmark contract for the September delivery sank to a day's low of $1,565 per tonne, the lowest level seen since mid-April. It closed a steep $150 down at $1,585.
The bale-out followed a five-month rally that peaked in May when prices touched 20-month highs of $2,700.

A volatile mix of low stocks, tight Latin American supply and worries that leading producer Brazil might have another damaging frost had lured a wave of speculative money to the coffee futures market.
But Tuesday's reversal took prices back to nearly half what they were on May 29.
The avalanche of selling emerged right from the opening bell.
"It's all fund selling," said one trader. "They were long in the market, now it's not clear whether they are short of it."
Stop-loss selling emerged as the price broke through $1,700 and then $1,610, before hitting a floor at $1,565.
Selling by producers was evident early in the session, but they later retreated as the market declined further.
No strong signs have yet emerged of the market turning, but it might rebound slightly in a technical correction to the heavy sell-off, analysts said.
Traders said the decline was purely chart-driven as London took little heed of a relatively calm New York futures market for premium arabica coffee.
They saw no fresh fundamental reasons behind London's fall.
But the winter in Brazil remains mild, with no frost forecast through July 22, while coffee stocks in Europe and the U.S. are building up again.
"More than that, we are going through a low consumption period," said one trader.

Coffee consumption traditionally dips during the northern hemisphere summer, and this year the market also faces a consumer reaction to the sharp retail price increases that followed the earlier futures rally from January lows of around $1,200.
Another trader said, "The speculators are going short. What we need now is the frost in Brazil, then the market will go up again."
The last crop-damaging frosts in Brazil were in June and July 1994.
